prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for its first experimental observation as protected edge conduction in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B038 as a single part with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and a citation limited to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall state and the time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulator as predicted and first observed. The chain is complete and short. Kane and Mele showed that spin-orbit coupling in a graphene-like band structure gives a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states. Molenkamp's group then measured quantized edge conductance in HgTe wells. The result has been reproduced for well over a decade by transport and by ARPES in several material families, and first-principles electronic-structure calculations now routinely classify and predict topological materials, which I can confirm from my own field. In answer to the chair's question on overlap, the 2016 prize honoured topological invariants in broken-time-reversal quantum Hall states and in defect-driven phase transitions. A time-reversal-invariant insulator whose topology is protected by spin-orbit coupling and a Z2 index, with helical edge modes in a real material, is a different object and was not covered by that citation. The citation I propose says exactly that and does not claim the three-dimensional field.
statement.case_against: The attribution is imperfect and I will not pretend otherwise. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal told Molenkamp which material and which well width to use, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional contributors (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan) are outside the trio. The three-name cap leaves a visible gap on the theory side, and the experimental side rests on one group for the first observation. A narrow citation reduces the gap but does not remove it. The 2016 overlap is a judgment call that some colleagues will weigh differently from me. Against B046, the clock has a cleaner two-name credit and a performance that is measured rather than argued, and that is a real advantage.

responses.point: Mark Pearce says he cannot judge B038 on condensed-matter grounds, relies on Olsson and me, and would support B038 as the second part or as the first choice if B046 stalls, provided a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is coherent.
responses.response: I think that condition can be met. Kane and Mele are the originators of the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall prediction. Molenkamp is the first and still the cleanest observer of the helical edge channels. The citation I have written ties the prediction to its first observation in time and in people, and it does not claim the three-dimensional work. I also accept that the two-part prize you raise does not fit under the three-person limit, because B038 alone uses all three names. So the choice is between B038 and B046 as single parts, not a combination. I do not ask you to rank B038 above B046 on field expertise. I ask only that the committee weighs the attribution gap and the novelty question on equal terms for both.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll recalls that the 2005 laureates were Glauber, Hall and Hansch and that Jun Ye was Hall's postdoc and not a laureate, which contradicts five colleagues who wrote that Ye shares the 2005 prize.
responses.response: My recollection agrees with Stefan's: the 2005 prize went to Glauber, Hall and Hansch, and Ye was in Hall's group but not a laureate. If that is right, the overlap argument against B046 is weaker than I and several others stated in round 1, and I withdraw the remark in my round-1 response that Ye already shares the 2005 prize. The remaining overlap with the comb is one of scientific lineage and not of a repeated laureate. That makes B046 harder for me to rank behind B038 on novelty grounds, and I now treat it as close to a tie on merit. The committee should still confirm the fact from the official records before relying on it, because my memory is not a primary source.

responses.point: Eva Olsson supports B038 with the citation kept narrow, and says the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap should be stated openly in the committee's rationale and not hidden. She also notes that the first experimental observation rests essentially on one group.
responses.response: I agree with her on both points and have adopted her wording in my citation. Where I would add something is on the experimental side: the one-group concern applies to the first observation only. Later InAs/GaSb transport work and the ARPES work on Bi-based materials confirm the topological class independently, though they do not repeat the original HgTe edge measurement in the same form. I would put the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal in the committee's rationale text as a recognised contribution that the three-name limit cannot accommodate. That is more honest than leaving it out, and it fits her view that a prize with a known weakness is better stated openly than defended.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth would regard B038 as a strong alternative if the committee can word a quantum-spin-Hall citation that honestly excludes the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and three-dimensional parts, and says she applies the same standard of related-prize overlap to both B038 and B046.
responses.response: I accept that standard and think it is the fair one. By the same test, B046 has a distinct invention in the magic-wavelength lattice, with a separate set of independent confirmations, so both candidates survive the overlap test. What separates them for me is the kind of result: B038 changes what we know about which materials can exist and how to find them, while B046 changes how precisely we can measure. Eva values the distinction between an instrument and a discovery in her own practice, so I take her view to be close to mine, even though she lands on B046 because of the cleaner attribution. I see the attribution problem as real but bounded, and the citation wording is where I propose to bound it.

uncertainties: Whether a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 insulator, without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang or the 3D contributors, is defended as honest by the committee or is seen as an attribution weakness that should make us wait.

Whether my recollection of the 2005 laureates is correct. I believe Ye was not a laureate, but I have not checked it against an official record, and priority details for both B038 and B046 are recalled from memory.
Whether the committee reads the 2016 prize on topological phases as already covering this theme. I have argued that it does not, but members who weigh it differently could reasonably prefer B046.
Whether the experimental side of B038 is deep enough, since the first observation rests on a single group even though the class has been confirmed elsewhere.
statement.conflict_note: I have no known collaboration, institutional tie or funding link to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero. I declare a scientific bias: my own field of electronic-structure theory benefits from the prediction of topological materials, and I would be glad to see that work recognised. That is a declaration and not a ground for recusal. This disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
